content: The Lourdes Medical Bureau is a medical organization located in Lourdes, France. It operates as an official entity within the Sanctuary of Our Lady of Lourdes and is exclusively managed by physicians. Its primary role is to conduct medical investigations into claims of miraculous cures associated with the Lourdes shrine. The term Medical Bureau also refers to a special assembly of doctors convened to examine such claims of unexplained healing. The apparitions at Lourdes occurred between February 11 and July 16, 1858. Following these events, reports of seemingly miraculous cures began to emerge. In 1859, Professor Henri Vergez from the Faculty of Medicine at Montpellier was appointed as a medical consultant to the Episcopal Commission of Inquiry to evaluate these claims. Vergez concluded that seven cases were genuinely inexplicable, leading to calls for the Roman Catholic Church to recognize these events as miracles. In 1883, a group called the Bureau des Constatations Médicales was established by doctors affiliated with the sanctuary, serving as the precursor to the current Medical Bureau. Its first head was Baron Dunot de Saint-Maclou. In 1905, Pope Pius X mandated that claims of miraculous cures at Lourdes undergo a rigorous investigative process, prompting the formal establishment of the Lourdes Medical Bureau. The bureau is currently led by a single physician, Dr. Patrick Theillier. Its office is modestly located on the second floor of the Accueil Jean Paul II building within the Domain, the consecrated grounds surrounding the shrine. Any practicing or visiting doctors in Lourdes may apply for membership in the bureau. Additionally, nurses, physiotherapists, pharmacists, and other allied health professionals are eligible to join. Members receive a distinctive badge featuring a red cross on a white background with the word Credo (I believe). Membership is open to individuals of any religious affiliation or none. Members are encouraged to notify the bureau of their visits to Lourdes. The bureau publishes a quarterly journal, Fons Vitae (Fountain of Life), which is distributed to members, along with case reports of interest. Approximately 35 claims of cures are brought to the bureau's attention annually, most of which are quickly dismissed. However, three to five cases each year undergo more thorough investigation. A Medical Bureau is convened, comprising doctors present in Lourdes at the time of the alleged cure. The investigation involves examining the patient, reviewing medical records, and analyzing test results, which may include biopsies, X-rays, CT scans, and blood tests. If further investigation is deemed necessary, the case is referred to the International Lourdes Medical Committee (CMIL), an international panel of around 20 medical experts from various disciplines and religious beliefs. CMIL meets annually, and a full investigation requires one of its members to meticulously review the case and immerse themselves in the relevant medical literature to ensure the application of up-to-date academic knowledge. The investigator may also consult colleagues. The findings are presented at a CMIL meeting, attended by the head of the Lourdes Medical Bureau and the Bishop of Tarbes and Lourdes. The cured individual is typically not present. For a cure to be recognized as medically inexplicable, several criteria must be met: The original diagnosis must be verified and confirmed beyond doubt. The condition must be deemed incurable with current medical means, although ongoing treatments do not disqualify the cure. The cure must occur in association with a visit to Lourdes, typically while in or near the shrine, though drinking or bathing in the water is not required. The cure must be immediate, with rapid resolution of symptoms and signs of the illness. The cure must be complete, with no residual impairment or deficit. The cure must be permanent, with no recurrence. CMIL does not declare a cure as miraculous; this determination is made by the Church. The bureau can only pronounce a cure as medically inexplicable. A full investigation takes a minimum of five years to ensure the permanence of the cure and may extend to ten or twelve years. It is acknowledged that, in rare cases, even advanced malignant diseases or severe infections may resolve spontaneously. CMIL votes on each case, requiring a two-thirds majority to declare a cure inexplicable. If CMIL deems a cure medically inexplicable, the case is referred to the bishop of the diocese where the cured individual resides. The bishop, in consultation with experts and the Vatican, decides whether the cure is miraculous. The bishop may reject the claim for any reason. Jacques Perrier, the Bishop of Tarbes and Lourdes, has expressed a desire for a new approach to recognizing cures in Lourdes, emphasizing that a pilgrimage to Mary is more than a journey to witness a miracle. Occasionally, cases dismissed by the Medical Bureau still gain fame and notoriety, such as the case of Jack Traynor. Notable Cases Jeanne Fretel: A 31-year-old student nurse from Rennes, France, suffering from tubercular peritonitis with complications for seven years, extreme emaciation, and oscillating fever. She was comatose when brought to Lourdes on May 10, 1948. After receiving a fragment of the Eucharist, she awoke and reported being instantly and permanently cured later that night. Her cure was officially recognized on November 11, 1950. Brother Léo Schwager: A 28-year-old from Fribourg, Switzerland, with multiple sclerosis for five years. He visited Lourdes on April 30, 1952, and his cure was recognized on December 18, 1960. Alice Couteault (née Alice Gourdon): A 34-year-old from Bouillé-Loretz, France, with multiple sclerosis for three years. She visited Lourdes on May 15, 1952, and her cure was recognized on July 16, 1956. Marie Bigot: A 32-year-old from La Richardais, France, with arachnoiditis of the posterior fossa, causing blindness, deafness, and hemiplegia. She visited Lourdes on October 8, 1953, and October 10, 1954. Her cure was recognized on August 15, 1956. Ginette Nouvel (née Ginette Fabre): A 26-year-old from Carmaux, France, with Budd-Chiari syndrome (supra-hepatic venous thrombosis). She visited Lourdes on September 21, 1954, and her cure was recognized on May 31, 1963. Elisa Aloi (later Elisa Varcalli): A 27-year-old from Patti, Italy, with tuberculous osteoarthritis and fistulae in her right leg. She visited Lourdes on June 5, 1958, and her cure was recognized on May 26, 1965. Juliette Tamburini: A 22-year-old from Marseilles, France, with femoral osteoperiostitis and fistulae for ten years. She visited Lourdes on July 17, 1959, and her cure was recognized on May 11, 1965. Vittorio Micheli: A 23-year-old from Scurelle, Italy, with a pelvic sarcoma so large that his left thigh became detached from the socket, leaving his leg paralyzed. After taking the waters at Lourdes on June 1, 1963, he was free of pain and able to walk. By February 1964, the tumor had disappeared, the hip joint had recalcified, and he returned to normal life. His cure was recognized on May 26, 1976. Serge Perrin: A 41-year-old from Lion d’Angers, France, with recurrent right hemiplegia and ocular lesions due to bilateral carotid artery disorders. He experienced sudden symptoms, including partial paralysis, impaired speech, and vision, beginning in February 1964. By 1970, he was wheelchair-bound and nearly blind. During a pilgrimage to Lourdes in April 1970, he felt a sudden warmth, regained his vision, and was able to walk unaided. His cure was recognized on June 17, 1978. Delizia Cirolli (later Delizia Costa): A 12-year-old from Paterno, Italy, with Ewing’s sarcoma of the right knee. Her doctors recommended amputation, but her mother refused and took her to Lourdes on December 24, 1976. Upon returning to Italy, her tumor regressed completely, though her tibia required corrective surgery. Her cure was recognized on June 28, 1989. She later became a nurse. Jean-Pierre Bély: A 51-year-old Frenchman with multiple sclerosis. He visited Lourdes on October 9, 1987, and his cure was recognized on February 9, 1999. Dr. Patrick Theillier Dr. Patrick Theillier is the twelfth physician to lead the Lourdes Medical Bureau. He earned his medical degree from Lille in 1964. Medical Care of Visitors The Lourdes Medical Bureau is not responsible for the direct medical care of pilgrims and visitors. General practitioners and the local hospital in Lourdes handle medical care. Many pilgrim groups, especially those with sick members, bring their own volunteer doctors and nurses to provide care. The Domain includes a treatment area called the Dispensary, located in the Accueil Jean Paul II. It is equipped for minor injuries and emergencies, including resuscitation facilities, airway equipment, and a defibrillator. It also has a small electric ambulance. The Dispensary operates during daylight hours and is staffed by nurses.
